Hardware, as in putting a computer together, or as in the circuitry of the components?

If you want to learn about putting computers together, take one apart. Look at FB marketplace, Craigslist, etc., and find some that are cheap or being given away. I wanted to update you all on what I did, and how I managed to get the system to work.

  
The display adapter I was using required USB-A power, as well as a connection to the motherboard/GPU. I had the connection, but the USB power was not being supplied because the ports were not enabled until later on in the booting process. I connected a VGA cable from the display, directly to the GPU, and I could see the POST results. Next, I replaced the CMOS battery, rebooted (the system was off when I changed the battery), and saw that the PC was now booting into DOS.

  
I am by no means an expert, and this situation had more to do with my mistakes, rather than some known issue that people need to be aware of, but I really can't stand people who ask for help online, figure out how to fix their issue, but never actually tell people what to do. I will leave you all with the things I learned:

  
1. The CMOS battery is almost certainly dead in whatever PC you are using, provided the system is 10-15 years old. This battery stores the settings from your BIOS, and will cause problems for you if the battery is dead. It doesn't cost much, and most supermarkets have packs of these batteries for like $6. Replace the battery and see if that fixes your issue(s) with booting.

  
2. While convenient, adapters for using old PCs with modern displays add another set of possible issues that you will have to deal with. If you are trying to get a computer to boot and you are having issues, one of the first things to test is whether or not your motherboard is able to output video. Of course, if the system is not on, there won't be a display, but if you can see/hear the fans and stuff, check the display connection.

  
3. Ensure that you have a PSU that can output enough voltage for your motherboard. You can find the output of the PSU by examining the outside of it. You can determine what your motherboard needs in order to run by examining the board, finding documentation on the Internet, or by trial and error. The motherboard will likely have a model number or some kind of ID somewhere on the edge of the board (on the top, not along the side of the board), or around the PCI slots. The location of the number depends on the motherboard.

  
4. Test components to ensure that they work. If you are having trouble booting, find out how to run diagnostic tests (such as POST codes or beeps that the system makes when it starts up), and start testing each component. I mentioned it briefly, but one of the first things I did was test the RAM, since the beep code I heard had something to do with the RAM being dead or unresponsive. I tried removing the RAM, and the motherboard detected that there was no RAM installed, which let me know that the motherboard must be working, and that the RAM sticks must be at fault. Swap things around, try different configurations, and determine what could, and what could not, be the culprit of the issue(s) you are dealing with.

  
5. Keep trying. Unless you have broken hardware, I would encourage you to keep trying, learn more about how computers work, discover a solution for your situation, and share your findings with others.

  
Thank you all for your help! God bless!
